description_full: Restaurant Brands International Inc. operates as a quick service restaurant company in Canada, the United States, and internationally. It operates through six segments: Tim Hortons, Burger King, Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen, Firehouse Subs, International, and Restaurant Holdings. The company owns and franchises Tim Hortons, a coffee and baked good restaurant chain that offers beverages, sandwiches, wraps, flatbread pizzas, and others; Burger King, a quick service hamburger restaurant chain that offers flame-grilled hamburgers, chicken, and other sandwiches; Popeyes, a quick service chicken concept that offers a Louisiana style menu, including fried bone-in chicken, chicken sandwiches, chicken tenders, wings, fried shrimp, and regional items; and Firehouse Subs, which offers subs with meats and cheese, as well as chili, soups, soft drinks, and other sides. Restaurant Brands International Inc. was founded in 1954 and is headquartered in Miami, Florida.

Each employee generates $27K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $3K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 16× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Restaurant Brands International is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $35.6B market cap on $9.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 12% against a 7% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 69% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.4B in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.21× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.3× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.1×.

Shareholder yield of 3.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 23% operating margin runs 16pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.83x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.8% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 7% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.52, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $205.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 57% in the 2020 crash and 24% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades only 3% below its DCF fair value of $79.86, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $41.28 to $147 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: EV/EBITDA 14.8 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 24.5 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 32% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 25 covering analysts target $85.32 on average, 10% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.31).
It runs a 69% gross margin and converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.21x.
ROE of 21% is amplified by 7.0x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.3x net debt to EBITDA ($1.0B of cash against $13.3B of debt), with interest covered 3.1x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.79 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The current ratio of 0.98 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.2% over 3 years, 13.7% over 5 years and 8.8% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 66%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 12.5% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 5% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 2.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 27, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.3%, and institutions hold 99%.
It returns 3.1% a year to shareholders (3.3% in dividends).
The share count has grown 2.4% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 11 consecutive years, raising it 2.9% a year over the last five.
people: With about 53,500 employees, each generates about $176K of revenue, 0.5x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 20.6% a year.
That works out to $27K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.8M (16x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
